item.title: PLA's 'silent drills' around Taiwan region? There is little to speculate about: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-11 23:59:00
Illustration: Chen Xia/GT Rather than obsessively scrutinizing situation maps and speculating about every movement, the DPP authorities should recognize an indisputable fact: In the fight against separatism and for national reunification, the PLA will never be absent and will never hesitate to act. Any separatist attempt to seek "Taiwan independence" by relying on external forces or military means will face severe punishment and is doomed to fail. Recently, a map dotted with red markers has become a hot topic on the island of Taiwan. It began when diehard "Taiwan independence" separatist Joseph Wu posted the map on social media, claiming that the Chinese People's Liberation Army (PLA) Navy and China Coast Guard (CCG) had "deployed 100+ vessels in the western Pacific." Two US think tanks jointly released a report, using a string of "may be" to speculate that the PLA was conducting a "major, unannounced military exercise." Taiwan region's so-called defense minister then followed suit, distorting the nature of these activities and smearing the PLA's normal maritime operations as "undermining" regional "peace and stability." Various forces have played along, taking turns speculating about and hyping the purported "silent drills," their objectives and details. The whole episode reeks of a calculated political effort to deliberately stoke tensions. There is little mystery here that warrants such excessive speculation. Whether it is the series of military exercises including "Joint Sword" and "Strait Thunder," or regular naval patrols, and law-based maritime law enforcement patrols by the CCG, they are all legitimate arrangements within China's sovereignty - lawful, reasonable, and beyond dispute. Take the PLA Navy's Liaoning aircraft carrier group training in the western Pacific, for example. China's Ministry of National Defense has publicly stated that the training was part of the PLA's annual routine schedule, was not directed at any specific country or target, and was consistent with international law and practice. Not to mention that the decision on whether to conduct military exercises, when to hold them and whether to release relevant information rests entirely with the PLA. Such decisions are made independently in accordance with China's defense needs and the situation across the Taiwan Straits, without any obligation to report to or seek approval from any other party. By deliberately portraying legitimate activities that have been clearly identified by official statements and are part of routine training arrangements as a "mysterious, unannounced military exercise," and repeatedly speculating about and sensationalizing this fabricated concept, certain forces are essentially trying to stoke public anxiety. In addition, years of exercises conducted under explicit code names and announced in coordinated public releases have made the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) authorities accustomed to a familiar playbook for managing public opinion on the island. Military activities around the Taiwan Straits are now shifting from periodic, concentrated operations to an around-the-clock, regularized presence. As early as April 2025, when the PLA Eastern Theater Command conducted joint exercises without an official code name, experts pointed out that such drills "have become routine and are nothing out of the ordinary for the PLA." Those with a guilty conscience can be startled by even the sound of ordinary footsteps. The Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) authorities' alarmist reaction to the "red-dot map" exposes their helplessness in the face of the new normal across the Taiwan Straits. They can neither deny the sovereign legitimacy of the People's Liberation Army's (PLA) operations nor rely on their old tactics to cope with a military presence that has defied their expectations. All they can do is turn a single map into a political spectacle, manufacture panic out of "silence," and falsely label the PLA's legitimate operations as "undermining peace and stability." For the majority of Taiwan compatriots, however, the PLA's regular presence around the Taiwan Straits serves to constrain the room for reckless moves by "Taiwan independence" separatist forces through sustained, visible and predictable deterrence, reducing the likelihood of miscalculation and dangerous adventurism. The stronger the deterrent capability of the people's armed forces, the more solid the guarantee that Taiwan residents can stay away from the ravages of war and enjoy peaceful, stable lives. This is a truth that cannot be turned on its head by a few slogans about "undermining peace and stability." The DPP authorities have repeatedly hyped the so-called "silent military drills," hoping to prolong their political survival by stoking tensions. Yet such tactics cannot stop the balance of power across the Straits from continuing to shift in a direction favorable to national reunification. If the "Taiwan independence" separatist forces were truly as confident as they claim, why would they be so unnerved by routine naval activities at sea? Their anxiety reveals that they are acutely aware of their predicament in going against the tide of history and deeply fearful of the balance of strength across the Straits and the direction of public sentiment. What they fear is not any particular military exercise or drill, but an overarching trend that is beyond their control. Let us put it more plainly: The PLA's regular presence around the Taiwan Straits will not change because of the political hype surrounding a "red-dot map," nor will it be halted by a chorus of accusations about "undermining peace and stability." Rather than obsessively scrutinizing situation maps and speculating about every movement, the DPP authorities should recognize an indisputable fact: In the fight against separatism and for national reunification, the PLA will never be absent and will never hesitate to act. Any separatist attempt to seek "Taiwan independence" by relying on external forces or military means will face severe punishment and is doomed to fail. National reunification is the ultimate outcome that leaves no room for speculation.

item.title: 77 years on, an ever-stronger PLA Air Force contributes to peace
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-11 23:56:00
China's Bayi Aerobatic Team flies over Great Wall to mark Air Force's 77th anniversary Photo: Li Hao/Global Times Wednesday marked the 77th anniversary of the founding of the Chinese People's Liberation Army (PLA) Air Force. After more than seven decades of development, the PLA Air Force has steadily advanced toward its strategic goal of "integrating air and space capabilities as well as coordinating offensive and defensive operations." With domestically developed new warplanes entering service as they are upgraded, the service has built an air combat force with a complete aircraft lineup, clear division of labor and efficient coordination, with modernization and system-based combat capability rising steadily. On Friday, six J-10 jets from the Chinese Air Force August 1st aerobatics team flew over the Great Wall as an anniversary tribute. On Monday, CCTV News' military channel released new footage offering a close-up, multi-angled look at the GJ-11 stealth drone, revealing its high-stealth characteristics, a buildup to the anniversary. Military affairs experts told the Global Times on Wednesday that in the new era, the Air Force's system-based combat capability has undergone profound changes and made great leaps. A series of broader international operations have also pushed domestic air power from "able to fly" toward "able to deploy far, coordinate across services and operate in unfamiliar environments." Building its force system for the future and accelerating modernization, the Air Force remains a defender of national sovereignty, security and development interests, and a steadfast guardian of peace and stability. System empowerment According to the CCTV News, looking back to the 1949 military parade marking the founding of the People's Republic of China, there were so few aircraft that they had to fly past twice to fill out the formation. After 77 years of hard work, the PLA Air Force started from that difficult position and gradually built a mature air and space combat system, completing a great strategic transition from homeland air defense to integrating air and space capabilities as well as coordinating offensive and defensive operations, Zhang Junshe, a Chinese military affairs expert, told the Global Times. In this transition, the main combat equipment system has continued to build and develop. With the public debut of the J-35A medium stealth multirole fighter, the Air Force's traditional "three swordsmen," the J-20 stealth fighter, J-16 fighter and J-10C fighter, have expanded and upgraded into a new "four swordsmen" lineup that includes two types of stealth fighters, CCTV reported. The four "swordsmen" form a new combination of the Air Force's aviation new-quality combat power, shaping a new air combat style of networked, coordinated air superiority and precision strikes across multiple aircraft types, CCTV reported. Zhang stressed that modern air combat is no longer a duel between single aircraft but a contest of systems. No matter how capable a single platform is, it can still create a weak link and struggle against complex, diverse battlefield threats. Deep integration and system empowerment across multiple services and aircraft types are essential, Zhang said. Fighters, bombers, early warning aircraft, tankers, electronic warfare aircraft, transport aircraft, reconnaissance drones and stealth drones each perform their roles and work closely together to build a solid air and space defense line, CCTV said. Beyond a complete equipment system, Zhang added, the Air Force's information hub is now stronger. Early warning aircraft serve as airborne command hubs, and data links act as the neural system, closely linking stealth fighters, drones, ground radar and air defense systems to achieve seamless connection between "seeing far" and "striking accurately." At the same time, new-quality combat forces are accelerating. High-stealth reconnaissance-strike drones operate alongside crewed fighters, pushing air and space confrontation into a new stage of intelligence and precision. The Air Force has all-domain offensive and defensive capability, not only with strong air superiority but also with breakthroughs in strategic early warning, long-range precision strikes, air and missile defense and strategic projection, achieving all-domain reach and combat capability, the expert said. CCTV reported that a modern strategic air force's combat power rests not only on advanced aviation equipment but on five core branches - aviation, ground-to-air missile, radar, airborne and electronic countermeasures - each performing its role in coordinated fashion, building a comprehensive, three-dimensional air and space defense system that is the core support for system-based air combat. An article from Outlook Weekly reposted by the Air Force's WeChat account said that at the upcoming 16th Airshow China in Zhuhai, Guangdong Province in December, the Air Force will maintain a system-based approach, coordinating static displays and flight performances to highlight iterative upgrades of main combat equipment. The share of new-quality combat forces will increase, and multiple main combat platforms will make their debuts. Exhibits will cover reconnaissance, early warning, air defense, support, airborne operations, unmanned applications, intelligent equipment and munitions, fully presenting the service's equipment renewal and evolving combat system. Growing global engagement On Wednesday, the PLA Air Force officially opened accounts on Facebook, YouTube, Instagram and X. The accounts will publish English short videos and posts on the Air Force's international exchanges, humanitarian operations and joint training, giving overseas audiences a more authentic, three-dimensional and comprehensive view of the PLA Air Force. Over the past year, the Air Force's external exchanges have widened and deepened. One of the highlights was that in August, the Air Force sent fighters, tankers, special mission aircraft and helicopters as a system to the China-Egypt Eagles of Civilization 2026 joint air training, focusing on air combat tactics, air superiority operations and combat search and rescue, along with force employment drills. During the training, PLA J-16s conducted air combat drills against Egyptian MiG-29 and Rafale fighters. A Chinese military affairs expert told the Global Times that the exercise marked China's first deployment of the J-16 and Egypt's first participation by Rafale fighters, reflecting a relatively high level of mutual trust and a considerable standard of joint training. Zhang said international joint training sessions enable the PLA Air Force to further turn equipment advantages into system capabilities, pushing domestic air power from "able to fly" toward "able to deploy far, coordinate across services and operate in unfamiliar environments." It tested and improved long-range projection and support, and honed system-based combat tactics and capabilities. It accumulated operational experience in foreign environments and drove continuous tactical upgrading, and spurred industrial development. Overseas users' operating habits, maintenance conditions and mission needs feed back into modular design, logistic supply and lifecycle support, ultimately benefiting domestic fielding, Zhang said. Beyond joint training, the PLA Air Force serves as an emissary of China's image and responsibility as a major power, observers noted. In September, an Air Force Y-20 transport aircraft carried multiple batches of relief supplies to Nepal for emergency humanitarian aid after mudslide disasters. In February, the August 1st Aerobatic Team performed in Singapore, its first public appearance there after switching to the J-10C. The complex and spectacular performance won wide praise. Song Zhongping, a Chinese military affairs expert, told the Global Times that an air force is a concentrated expression of a country's military and industrial capability. Along with the Air Force's growing strength, Chinese-made fighters are gaining global recognition and broad export prospects. This year, Uzbekistan's official media reported that the country had procured the J-10CE from China. Beyond that, countries including Bangladesh and Indonesia are reportedly advancing procurement or showing interest in the fighter. Song said that while the use of Chinese aviation equipment continues to increase in foreign trade cooperation, China's arms exports only contribute to regional peace and stability and help countries improve their foundational capacity for self-defense, just as the Air Force's modernization serves to safeguard national sovereignty, security and development interests and defend peace and stability. Committed to being a builder of world peace, a contributor to global development and a defender of the international order, the Chinese Air Force's flight paths across the world contribute important strength to safeguarding world peace and promoting win-win cooperation, Outlook Weekly said. "From trailing behind to running neck and neck, the PLA Air Force has traveled an extraordinary path. As China's technological and economic strength continues to grow, the Air Force and aviation industry are expected to develop further and rapidly, bringing greater miracles and more opportunities in the good for world peace," Song said.

item.title: China's clean energy products win global praise for driving green transition at COP31
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-11 23:52:00
The China Pavilion at COP31 Photo: IC As world leaders gather in Türkiye for COP31 amid renewed disputes over climate finance and a retreat from global climate cooperation by the US, China is emerging as an increasingly influential force in the fight against climate change. Its booming clean energy industry has made green technologies more affordable for developing countries, drawing praise from Western climate leaders even as Washington and Brussels impose trade barriers on Chinese products - exposing a growing contradiction between climate ambitions and economic protectionism. Chinese Vice President Han Zheng, as President Xi Jinping's special representative, met with UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on Tuesday on the sidelines of the Antalya Leaders' Summit at the 31st meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, per the Xinhua News Agency. China is committed to setting clear targets and ensuring their implementation, and stresses the need to be true in word and resolute in deed, which will continue to provide valuable stability and certainty for global climate governance, Han said. China has worked with the United Nations to advance international cooperation on addressing climate change, firmly upholding and fully implementing the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change and the Paris Agreement, vigorously promoting South-South cooperation on climate change, and actively supporting the UN-led Early Warnings for All initiative, he said. The global response to climate change currently faces numerous challenges, Han said, noting that developing countries, in particular, are confronted with difficulties including funding shortages, technological shortcomings and inadequate capacity in implementing their nationally determined contributions, challenges that the international community must address together. At this year's COP31, former US secretary of state John Kerry, who also served as special presidential envoy for climate, told the Guardian that China is leading the world in moving away from fossil fuels, and the rest of the globe - including the US - must now follow. "The only country that has hugely accelerated [in embracing low-carbon power and rapid electrification] is China. The rest of the world is stumbling along while Mother Nature is sending us more powerful signals every week, every day," said Kerry. Similarly, Chris Bowen, COP31 President of Negotiations and Australian Minister for Climate Change and Energy, praised China's contribution to making clean energy more affordable worldwide on Tuesday. Bowen made the remarks at a side event titled "Ecological Civilization and Beautiful China Practice" at the China Pavilion, according to a China News report. Speaking at a COP31 side event, Huang Runqiu, China's minister of ecology and environment, highlighted China's progress in green transformation, pollution control and environmental conservation, citing a series of figures: the country has completed ultra-low-emission upgrades for 1.17 billion kilowatts of coal-fired power capacity and 1 billion tons of crude steel production capacity, according to a readout published by the ministry on Wednesday. China has also led the world in electric vehicle production and sales for 11 consecutive years. Over the past five years, average concentrations of fine particulate matter (PM2.5) have fallen by 20 percent, while the number of days with severe air pollution has dropped by 25 percent, said Huang. This year's COP comes after a year of devastating extreme weather, marked by soaring temperatures and deadly heat waves across Europe and beyond, while the absence of the United States has further complicated global efforts to tackle climate change. COP observers and international media have turned the spotlight back on China, wondering if "China will finally step into the leadership role" in global climate action, as the Guardian asked. The growing international recognition of China's role in tackling climate change reflects the country's rising economic and technological strength, according to a Chinese expert. Once viewed largely as a costly undertaking, the fight against climate change has increasingly become an economic opportunity, driven in part by China's rapid advances in clean energy technology and manufacturing, Bao Cunkuan, a professor in the Department of Environmental Sciences and Engineering at Fudan University, told the Global Times. For developing countries, particularly those in the Global South, where energy costs can place a heavy burden on economic development, the expansion of China's renewable energy industry has helped make clean power more affordable and accessible, allowing countries to pursue economic growth while reducing emissions, said Bao. As for growing calls for China to assume a greater leadership role in global climate governance, the expert said the country's influence should be measured not by whether it formally takes the lead, but by its capabilities and concrete achievements in advancing the green transition. China actions At a press conference last month, Li Gao, vice minister of ecology and environment, said that China was calling for the COP31 climate summit to focus on implementing existing commitments and addressing both longstanding gaps in emissions cuts and climate finance, as well as new challenges from unilateralism and protectionism. China is by far the world's largest producer of the solar panels, wind turbines, batteries and electric cars needed to cut emissions. However, that technology is increasingly seen as a threat by countries concerned about the competitive impact on their local industries, per Reuters. The US has imposed steep tariffs on Chinese solar products and electric cars while the European Union has done the same for autos, imposed restrictions on some solar components and is investigating a major Chinese wind company. Steep tariffs imposed by the United States and European countries on Chinese clean energy products risk undermining the very climate goals they have pledged to pursue, said Ma Jun, director of the Institute of Public and Environmental Affairs. With much of the world already lagging in the transition to renewable energy, such protectionist measures threaten to drive up costs, slow the adoption of affordable green technologies and hinder global efforts to combat climate change, Ma said. By prioritizing domestic industrial interests over the urgent need to accelerate the energy transition, Western governments risk turning trade protectionism into another barrier to global climate action. According to a Reuters analysis, China sent $132 billion in clean technology and investment to the developing world last year, by far the largest contribution to carbon-dioxide reduction of any country. That figure nearly matched the total of grants, loans and private finance that all wealthy countries sent to poorer ones in 2024 to help fight climate change. Ma said he had spoken with climate experts from Pakistan who described how falling prices had made Chinese solar panels increasingly affordable for ordinary households, prompting more families to embrace the technology. By installing rooftop solar panels, these households have been able to reduce their dependence on an unreliable power grid and gain greater control over their electricity supply. Beyond making daily life easier, access to affordable, reliable electricity has also created opportunities for families to start small businesses, earn a living and improve their economic prospects, Ma said. Therein lies the irony of global climate politics: Wealthy nations have yet to fulfill their climate finance commitments to developing countries, even as they lecture China over its emissions and environmental record. Yet when China offers a more affordable path to decarbonization through its clean energy technologies, those same governments respond by slapping tariffs on Chinese products. For all their "lofty" rhetoric about saving the planet, it is becoming increasingly clear who is driving the green transition forward — and who is standing in its way, said experts.

item.title: Chinese FM holds positive, constructive phone talks with US secretary of state
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-11 23:41:00
China US Photo: VCG Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi held a phone conversation with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Wednesday, during which the two sides had an in-depth exchange of views on China-US relations and interactions between the two countries' heads of state. The conversation was positive and constructive, according to a statement released by China's Foreign Ministry on Wednesday. Wang, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, said that the hard-won momentum toward stability in China-US relations represents a rational choice made by the two major countries based on their respective and shared interests. China's policy toward the US remains stable and consistent, Wang said, adding that China is willing to strengthen communication and cooperation with the US, properly handle differences and sensitive issues, support each other in successfully hosting the 2026 APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting and the G20 Summit and translate the vision of building a constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability into action. Global Times

item.title: GT Voice: What Washington risks by tightening tech curbs on China?
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-11 22:26:00
The photo taken from atop the Washington Monument on Nov. 17, 2025 shows the construction site where the East Wing of the White House was recently demolished, while construction crews prepare the area for the White House's new ballroom, in Washington, D.C., the United States. (Xinhua/Hu Yousong) Reuters reported on Tuesday, citing three people familiar with the matter, that Microsoft, other companies and trade groups have pressed Washington to halt plans to bar imports from China of new models of optical transceivers, a key component in artificial intelligence (AI) data centers. This little-noticed component is emerging as an unexpected test for the AI industry in the US. These discussions are taking place against a sensitive backdrop. Some are seizing on the controversy surrounding Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to stir unfounded fears and suspicion about Chinese technology, apparently seeking to build momentum for another round of restrictions on China's tech sector. Viewing technology through an ever-expanding national security lens could ultimately undermine the AI development the US is seeking to accelerate. Optical transceivers may seem like a minor, separate issue, largely unrelated to the current debate. Yet the episode is telling a sign of what is at stake. Whenever US-China technology supply chains face the prospect of disruption, US tech companies are often among the first to feel the pressure. Why are Microsoft and other US companies so alarmed by reports that Washington may restrict these imports? The answer lies in the structure of the global supply chains. Chinese manufacturers occupy a substantial position in the global optical transceiver market. According to Counterpoint Research, Chinese optical module manufacturers account for nearly two-thirds of global unit supply and approximately 60 percent of global optical datacom transceiver revenue. Can the US afford to build its data centers without Chinese optical transceivers? These components enable data to travel at the speed of light over fiber-optic cables, making them essential to data center operations. John Miller, an executive vice president of policy and general counsel of the Information Technology Industry Council, told Reuters that such a ban "really threatens to arguably grind" data center rollouts to a halt. This exposes a fundamental contradiction. The US is seeking to contain China's technological development through tighter restrictions and, in some areas, supply chain "decoupling." Yet it also wants to accelerate its own technological progress, which increasingly relies on Chinese-sourced materials and components, as well as access to the Chinese market. These two goals are increasingly at odds. As China's technological capabilities advance, Chinese companies are gaining a stronger foothold in the supply chains for components and critical technologies. At the same time, the expansion of the Chinese market is creating opportunities for US companies. The technology industries of the two countries remain deeply intertwined, reflecting substantial scope for mutual benefits. The more China advances technologically, the sharper the contradiction facing Washington becomes, and its efforts to contain China are increasingly at odds with its own need for technological development. The optical transceiver issue shows how acute this contradiction has already become. As Miller warned, a ban on Chinese suppliers could bring US data center rollouts to a halt. Washington may therefore be nearing the point at which further restrictions would directly obstruct its own AI development. That is why Microsoft and other US companies are so alarmed. Yet the growing tendency in US public discourse to hype the so-called China threat and broaden the scope of national security concerns risks further disrupting supply chains from which the US tech industry itself stands to benefit from. If that happens, AI development in the US will be among the first to pay the price. The US should think twice. The optical transceiver should serve as a wake-up call, showing that there are limits to how far Washington can go in restricting Chinese technology before those restrictions begin to undermine its own interests. In the wake of the midterm elections, US data center development is facing mounting headwinds at home. Tightening restrictions on Chinese technology would only compound these obstacles. Efforts to curb China's technological progress may end up holding back US' own AI development.

item.title: China issues revised rules on human genetic resources management to strengthen biosecurity
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-11 21:33:00
A vial representing cell and gene therapies, an emerging field in biopharmaceutical innovation. Photo: VCG China's National Health Commission (NHC) on Wednesday published an updated version of the detailed implementation rules for the management of human genetic resources, tightening safeguards for national biosecurity and the public interest. The rules, revised from a document first issued in 2023, cover activities involving the collection, preservation and use of China's human genetic resources within the country, as well as providing such resources and information overseas, Xinhua News Agency reported. Human genetic resources generally refer to human organs, tissues and cells containing genetic materials such as DNA, as well as the genetic information derived from them. China's Ministry of State Security revealed that some overseas organizations have illegally collected human blood samples and sought access to genetic resources and research data under the guise of tourism, scientific research and medical testing. In 2025, Guangzhou Customs dismantled a major cross-border smuggling network involving pregnant women's blood samples that spanned 23 provincial-level regions. The smuggling ring illegally exported more than 100,000 samples, generating over 30 million yuan ($4.49 million). The NHC said on Wednesday that the revisions optimize relevant approval and filing procedures and strengthen the regulatory and supervision framework, aiming to ensure that human genetic resources are used in a standardized, secure, and efficient manner. Under the rules, activities involving human genetic resources must comply with relevant laws, regulations and other requirements. They must not endanger China's public health, national security or the public interest. Overseas individuals and organizations are prohibited from collecting or preserving China's human genetic resources within the country or providing such resources to overseas entities, according to the rules. Foreign organizations seeking to use China's human genetic resources for scientific research must comply with Chinese laws and regulations, and conduct their research in cooperation with Chinese institutions. Any entity conducting international collaborative research using China's human genetic resources must obtain approval from the NHC, the document said, adding that the export of human genetic resource materials - including their shipment, mailing or transportation out of China - also requires NHC approval, as well as completion of customs procedures. Global Times

item.title: Shanghai signs deals, Washington signs sanctions: 25 years after China joined the WTO, the world sees two logics
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-11 21:16:00
CIIE Photo: VCG On the 25th anniversary of the decision to admit China to the WTO at the Doha Ministerial Conference, the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission (USCC) posted a tweet claiming that "years of engagement and pressure failed to change Beijing's approach." It accused China of "distorting global markets, eroding US manufacturing, and undermining American businesses" through protectionism. Interestingly, on the very day this tweet was posted, the 9th China International Import Expo (CIIE) concluded in Shanghai. The expo drew participants from 162 countries and regions, with exhibition space exceeding 440,000 square meters. The total value of intended transactions reached $85.45 billion, a 2.3 percent year-on-year rise, and 485 new products made their debut at the event. China has demonstrated through concrete actions that its market remains open. This is not just a slogan; it is a window of openness that continues to swing wide for the world. On this side of the window are orders, product debuts, and the sincerity of an open market. Customs data from November 10 speaks volumes: In the first 10 months of 2026, China's exports grew by 17.6 percent year-over-year, while imports rose by 23.6 percent - with imports growing 6 percentage points faster than exports. On the other side of the window, the picture could not be more different. The EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) officially entered its paid implementation phase this past January. Meanwhile, citing "overcapacity" and "forced labor," the US has successively launched Section 301 investigations against 60 economies, including China, and ramped up tariff barriers, building ever-higher trade walls. This exposes a reality: For certain countries, the "free trade" they seek comes with a precondition - they must win. Once they find themselves losing, the rules can be changed, tariffs can be imposed, and investigations can be launched. The "rules-based international order" is nothing more than a euphemism for "my way or the highway." "The wave of openness at the CIIE coexists with and plays out against the trade barriers erected by the US and the EU - a microcosm of the most significant contradiction in global trade today," Li Yong, an executive council member of the China Society for WTO Studies, told the Global Times on Wednesday. "The original intent of trade rules should be to drive the qualitative and quantitative growth of trade and promote the free flow of goods, rather than to artificially create obstacles or erect exclusionary barriers," said Li. Twenty-five years since China's accession to the WTO, who is actually honoring their commitments, and who is changing the rules? For China, the answer is found in the exhibition booths at the CIIE; for the US and EU, the answer lies in Section 301 and CBAM. China has generated $85.45 billion in import orders during the CIIE, fulfilling its commitment to openness through market dividends. Since joining the WTO, China has reduced its overall tariff rate to 7.3 percent, eliminated all foreign investment access restrictions in the manufacturing sector, implemented zero tariffs on 100 percent of tariff lines for all least-developed countries with which it has diplomatic relations, and expanded its zero-tariff treatment to cover all 53 African countries with which it has diplomatic relations. Li stated that the most authoritative and objective measure of whether an economy is adhering to its multilateral commitments upon accession to the WTO is the organization's long-term official assessment. Over the years, the WTO's overall evaluation of China's fulfillment of its WTO obligations has consistently been highly positive, demonstrating that China has fully and even exceedingly fulfilled its accession commitments and strictly adhered to multilateral trade rules. The US side's statements are entirely one-sided and constitute a smear campaign that does not reflect the facts. Since China joined the WTO, the concept of openness has evolved. A high-level opening-up has never been a mandatory obligation for any single country, but rather a multilateral responsibility that all WTO members should uphold. Over the past 25 years, China has delivered tangible outcomes including $85.45 billion worth of CIIE deals to prove that openness delivers win-win results. Some countries, by contrast, resort to trade barriers to show their priority is not whether rules are fair, but whether they remain on the winning side. The world has clearly seen two sets of logic at play: One is focused on making the pie bigger, the other on snatching others' share of the pie. One is signing trade deals; the other is imposing sanctions. The lights have dimmed in Shanghai's exhibition halls, yet the doors remain open. The tweets from Washington have run their course, yet more locks keep being added. Which logic will stand the test of time? The market is already casting its vote with orders.

item.title: China updates standards for key robot component amid rising demand
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-11 21:06:00
Visitors observe a humanoid robot on display at the Shanghai International Intelligent Home Expo in Shanghai on September 28, 2026. Photo: VCG China has revised two national standards governing harmonic drive reducers, a key transmission component used in industrial and humanoid robots, in a move aimed at improving product quality and supporting the development of its domestic precision machinery industry, the Guangming Daily reported. The standards, GB/T 12601-2026, covering basic terminology for harmonic gear drives, and GB/T 14118-2026, covering harmonic drive reducers, were highlighted at a technical seminar and standards launch conference held recently in Shengzhou, East China's Zhejiang Province. The revisions mark the first major updates to the two standards in more than three decades, the report noted. They are scheduled to take effect on April 1, 2027, according to China's National Standard Information Public Service Platform. Harmonic drive reducers are precision transmission devices installed in robot joints. They use controlled elastic deformation of a flexible gear to transmit motion and torque, allowing robots to achieve precise movements in a compact space. They are widely used in industrial robots, collaborative robots and humanoid robots. Their importance is expected to grow as humanoid robots develop. According to industry estimates, a single humanoid robot may require multiple harmonic reducers across its joints, making the component an important part of the industry's supply chain. China's harmonic reducer market was valued at approximately 3.8 billion yuan ($570 million) in 2025 and is expected to reach 4.8 billion yuan in 2026, according to estimates by industry research firm Zhiyan Consulting. Demand in the robotics sector is also projected to expand rapidly. Shipments of harmonic reducers for robots in China are expected to increase from 1.4 million units in 2025 to 20.7 million units by 2030, representing a compound annual growth rate of 72.4 percent, according to estimates by China Insights Consultancy. The expansion, however, comes with mounting competitive pressure on domestic manufacturers. For years, Japan's Harmonic Drive Systems and other overseas suppliers held a strong position in the high-end market. Chinese manufacturers have gradually expanded their presence through research and development, improvements in manufacturing processes and efforts to replace imported products. The progress has been significant, but competition is increasingly shifting from securing market share to improving product performance, reliability and cost efficiency. Against this backdrop, the two revised standards are expected to help address some of these challenges. The first, GB/T 12601-2026, establishes a unified set of terms used across the industry, helping researchers, manufacturers and testing institutions communicate and work with consistent definitions. The second, GB/T 14118-2026, sets out requirements for harmonic drive reducers, including product categories, quality requirements and testing procedures. In practical terms, it provides manufacturers and customers with a common benchmark for judging whether products meet the required standards. The revision also comes as China's broader robotics industry seeks to strengthen its domestic supply chain. In 2023, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology issued guidelines for the development of humanoid robots, identifying core components, including precision transmission systems, as important areas for technological progress.

item.title: Indian scientist praises China's openness to intl space cooperation as Pakistani astronaut's planned flight aboard Shenzhou-24 prompts media discussion in India
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-11 17:27:00
China's Shenzhou-21 and the Tiangong space station in the orbit Photo: IC A Pakistani astronaut is set to become the first foreign astronaut to visit the China Space Station, flying aboard China's Shenzhou-24 spacecraft. The planned flight has prompted discussions in Indian media about international space cooperation. In an exclusive response to the Global Times, an Indian scientist whose research project was selected for the China Space Station praised China's openness to international collaboration while acknowledging that political considerations and concerns about public perceptions have hindered work on his project. Jayant Murthy, principal investigator of the Spectroscopic Investigations of Nebular Gas (SING) project, which was selected in 2019 under a United Nations-China initiative to conduct experiments aboard the China Space Station, told the Global Times that international cooperation in space exploration is not merely desirable but necessary. "My experience with the SING mission is that, unfortunately, politics gets in the way of the collaboration," Murthy said in a written response to the Global Times. "Much of this is not even government policy but is due to an abundance of caution by people who don't want to make a wrong decision," he added, suggesting that a dedicated coordinating agency staffed by scientists could help advance the project. Murthy also expressed appreciation for China's willingness to open its space station to international researchers. "Chinese generosity in opening the CSS to collaboration is something that we should all take advantage of in building strong scientific and cultural links between our nations and I hope that more groups come forward," he said. His remarks came as Pakistan's upcoming participation in China's Shenzhou-24 crewed mission prompted discussion in Indian media about the growing importance of international partnerships in space exploration, beyond the pursuit of independent technological capabilities. In an analysis published on November 9, The Times of India examined the broader implications of Pakistan becoming the first foreign country to send an astronaut to China's Tiangong space station, placing the development in the context of evolving international space partnerships and India's own human spaceflight ambitions. The newspaper noted that the mission demonstrated China's ability to accommodate international astronauts aboard its independently developed space station. With the International Space Station approaching retirement, the China Space Station could increasingly provide another platform for countries seeking opportunities in human spaceflight and orbital scientific research, the report suggested. In a November 9 report titled "Shenzhou-24 mission: China opens its orbit to Pakistan's astronauts," Indian magazine The Week quoted space analyst Girish Linganna as saying that "For India, which is building its own human spaceflight capability, it is a reminder that the region's space race is now about international relations, not just space technology." Indian media attention to the mission reflects changes in the regional space landscape, Qian Feng, director of the Research Department at Tsinghua University's National Strategy Institute, told the Global Times. "India has long regarded itself as a leading space power in South Asia. Pakistan's upcoming breakthrough in human spaceflight through cooperation with China has prompted Indian media to reassess the country's own space cooperation strategy," Qian said. At a regular press conference on November 9, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun confirmed that a Pakistani astronaut would participate in the Shenzhou-24 mission as a payload specialist and return aboard the Shenzhou-23 spacecraft after completing a short-term stay in orbit. Guo said that exploring the vast universe and peacefully utilizing outer space are shared aspirations of humanity, adding that China has consistently advocated the peaceful use of outer space and actively pursued international space cooperation. In 2019, the China Manned Space Agency and the United Nations Office for Outer Space Affairs (UNOOSA) jointly announced the first batch of scientific experiments selected for implementation aboard the China Space Station. According to UNOOSA, nine projects involving 23 institutions from 17 countries were selected. Notably, Indian scientists were among the researchers selected to participate in the initiative. However, the project's implementation subsequently encountered difficulties involving export approvals from Indian authorities. In Murthy's latest response to the Global Times, Murthy did not provide an update on whether the export approval had been granted or whether the equipment had been shipped to China. His comments, however, offered a firsthand account of the nontechnical obstacles that have affected the project. Murthy emphasized that scientists should be able to cooperate across national boundaries, particularly given the substantial financial and technological resources required for space exploration. "When we do anything in space, we are working for all humanity and, because it is so expensive in money and resources, it is necessary for us all to collaborate and make the most use of the opportunities that we have," Murthy added. Qian said "such interference not only disrupts scientific research and deprives scientists of valuable experimental opportunities, but also undermines mutual trust in international scientific cooperation." China and India have complementary strengths in space exploration, with China possessing extensive experience in space station operations, human spaceflight and deep-space exploration, while India has developed capabilities in cost-effective satellite launches, remote sensing and lunar exploration, Qian said. "Space cooperation should not be overshadowed by narrow political considerations," Qian added.

item.title: Taiwan question brooks no external interference: mainland spokesperson on question about China-US discussions at APEC
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-11 12:20:00
Taiwan Affairs Office spokesperson Zhang Han When asked about discussions between China and the US on Taiwan-related issues during the APEC meetings, Zhang Han, a spokesperson for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, said on Wednesday that the Taiwan question is purely China's internal affair, which brooks no external interference. Zhang stressed that peace and stability across the Taiwan Straits can only be guaranteed by unequivocally opposing "Taiwan independence” and firmly upholding the one-China principle. Taiwan is part of China, and the one-China principle and the three China-US joint communiqués form the political foundation of China-US relations, the spokesperson noted. The Democratic Progressive Party authorities' attempts to seek “Taiwan independence” by relying on external forces will only turn Taiwan into a pawn in the hands of external forces, ultimately leaving it with no escape from the fate of being abandoned, Zhang said. Global Times
